Berlin's criminal gangs prey on refugees for new recruits

In case of paywall;

Berlin’s criminal gangs prey on refugees for new recruits City police and officials warn the struggle to integrate newcomers leaves them vulnerable by: Guy Chazan in Berlin

It was volunteer helpers at the refugee shelter at 282 Buckower Damm who first raised the alarm. They suspected that security guards at the converted school gym in Neukölln, a district of southern Berlin, were trying to recruit young migrants as drug dealers. Plain-clothes policemen sent there late last year confirmed the reports and the guards were promptly sacked.

Arnold Mengelkoch, Neukölln’s commissioner for migration, says it was not an isolated incident. “It is clear to us that some of the criminal families are on the hunt for new employees for their drug business along U-Bahn line 8,” he says, referring to a key hangout along a train route for drug pushers.

Germany is engaged in a historic effort to integrate the 1m migrants who flooded into the country last year. Authorities have scrambled to provide enough housing, food and language courses for the newcomers, many of whom are war refugees still reeling from hazardous odysseys through Europe. But full integration is taking longer than they expected — and, with frustration mounting, some refugees are becoming increasingly vulnerable to the allure of organised crime. Berlin police, prosecutors and municipal officials worry that people are already being sucked into the city’s thriving underworld, where big Arab clans dominate the drugs trade, prostitution and human trafficking. “People from Berlin come to them, speak to them in their language, and make them very tempting offers,” says Sjors Kamstra, a senior public prosecutor in Berlin. “They could say, ‘why rely on welfare handouts of €100 when you could stand by the U-Bahn and sell heroin?’ ”

The recruitment efforts are often along ethnic lines. For example, North African gangs are actively targeting newly arrived compatriots from the Maghreb, says Thomas Heilmann, Berlin’s justice minister. He adds that this has accelerated since the government tightened rules this year making it harder for migrants from Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia to obtain asylum.

“Gangs are taking advantage of the fact that many of these men will remain here illegally and so can easily be deployed for criminal activities,” Mr Heilmann says. Of 50 drug dealers arrested and imprisoned in Berlin over the winter, “a large proportion were refugees”, he adds.

The history of Berlin’s large Arab crime syndicates provides a cautionary tale about the importance of integrating asylum-seekers as quickly as possible. Many of Germany’s big Arab clans first arrived in the country in the 1980s, as refugees from Lebanon’s civil war. They were banned from working or obtaining drivers’ licences, while their children were not allowed to attend school.

“Nothing was done to integrate them, because it was thought they would only be here til the war ended,” says Dirk Jacob, a Berlinpolice investigator who specialises in organised crime. “They were pushed to the margins of society.”

As a result, some fell into a life of crime. Police say there are seven big Arab clans in Berlin involved in criminal activities, ranging from drug trafficking to attacks on cash machines and safe deposits. Their members have carried out some of the city’s most spectacular armed robberies, such as a 2014 heist at the high-end department store KaDeWe, in which masked men stole jewellery worth €800,000, and a 2010 attack on a poker tournament at Berlin’s Grand Hyatt Hotel.

Around a quarter of the 40-60 organised crime investigations conducted every year in Berlin are dominated by ethnic Arabs, Mr Jacob says. In other categories of crime, the picture is different — Mr Heilmann says house break-ins, for example, are the preserve of gangs from eastern Europe and Georgia. Crime is a particular problem in Neukölln, one of the most ethnically diverse and economically deprived boroughs in Germany. It has become a magnet for immigrants, who make up 43 per cent of the population, but social problems run deep. Neukölln’s unemployment rate is 15.2 per cent and among its foreign migrants it is twice as high, compared with Germany’s national average of 6.3 per cent. Juvenile delinquency is also rife in the borough. Authorities have identified 151 youths who commit on average more than 10 crimes a year — 54 per cent of them are of Arab descent, even though Arabs only make up 9 per cent of Neukölln’s population. “We can’t seem to reduce this proportion,” says Mr Mengelkoch. “Arab boys are really the hardest group for us.”

Germany’s refugee influx has caused a rise in this demographic group. “When you look at the crime statistics you find a huge pool of offenders, regardless of nationality and faith, among men aged between 16 and 25,” says Mr Jacob. “And we have a large number of unaccompanied young adult males in the [refugee] shelters who are in this age group.”

So far, Germany’s influx of foreigners has not led to an uptick in crime — in fact, statistics released this month showed an 18 per cent drop in the number of crimes committed by immigrants between January and March. Foreigners committed 69,000 crimes in total, according to the data, indicating they were no more likely to engage in criminal activity than Germans.

Mr Kamstra, the public prosecutor, says the new arrivals have so far had “no impact” on Berlin’s criminal landscape. But there is no denying the risk that some will end up as “errand boys” for the mob, he adds. “I try to put myself in their place — they come with nothing, they don’t speak German, they have no profession,” he says. “So such offers are tempting.”
